questions.prompt: What is the chapter's main claim?
choices: Two things can look alike in story or label while differing structurally underneath
Labels never matter at all
Comparison should be abandoned because everything is unique

explanation.gentle: The chapter warns that neat similarity can hide real differences in capability, exposure, and payoff.
explanation.direct: Taleb argues that rhetorical resemblance is weaker than structural resemblance when judging equivalence.
explanation.competitive: The same badge can still be hiding a different machine.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter distrust polished narratives?
choices: Because storytelling always lies
Because polished stories can compress away the asymmetries that matter
Because categories are useless in every case

explanation.gentle: The chapter worries that a neat story can hide the differences that really matter.
explanation.direct: Narrative polish is risky here because it can erase capability gaps, exposure gaps, or payoff gaps from view.
explanation.competitive: The prose can iron out the risk gap right before the pressure test arrives.

questions.prompt: What common misreading does the chapter reject?
choices: That comparison must go past the label
That two same-sounding things may differ underneath
That labels never matter in any way

explanation.gentle: The chapter is not saying labels are worthless.
explanation.direct: Taleb rejects semantic paralysis; labels can orient judgment, but they cannot finish it alone.
explanation.competitive: He is not banning categories. He is banning lazy verdicts based on them.

questions.prompt: Elena is comparing two candidates who look similar on paper, but one has a much stronger history of reality-tested work and a better downside profile. Which response best fits the chapter?
choices: Treat them as equivalent because the résumés share the same headline category
Compare what each candidate has actually done, survived, and exposed herself to before judging sameness
Avoid comparison completely because labels cannot be trusted at all

explanation.gentle: The chapter prefers structural comparison over paper similarity.
explanation.direct: The right move is to inspect capability, exposure, and payoff beneath the shared résumé label.
explanation.competitive: Audit the machinery instead of bowing to the badge.

questions.prompt: Which statement would the chapter reject most strongly?
choices: A polished shared description is enough to prove real equivalence
A category can start a comparison without finishing it
Two opportunities can share a title and still differ in payoff shape

explanation.gentle: The chapter attacks the belief that neat similarity settles the question.
explanation.direct: Taleb rejects stopping at rhetorical resemblance before structural sameness has been shown.
explanation.competitive: That answer lets the brochure impersonate the load test.

questions.prompt: What is structural comparison in this chapter?
choices: Comparing by category name alone
Comparing by hidden capability, exposure, and payoff beneath the label
Comparing only by how elegant the narrative sounds

explanation.gentle: Structural comparison looks underneath the shared description.
explanation.direct: The chapter asks what each thing can do, survive, and expose you to rather than how similar the summary sounds.
explanation.competitive: You compare the build, not the brochure.

questions.prompt: A team keeps calling two project paths basically the same because they fit the same bucket, even though one carries much worse downside and less flexibility. What pattern does this show?
choices: Helpful simplification
False sameness created by narrative compression
Proof that comparison is impossible

explanation.gentle: The team is letting a category hide a real structural difference.
explanation.direct: This matches the chapter's warning that labels can flatten away the asymmetries that matter.
explanation.competitive: They let the bucket do the thinking and erased the payoff gap.

questions.prompt: Why can two same-sounding options still be importantly different?
choices: Because labels never compress anything
Because shared description can hide different histories, exposures, and payoff structures
Because similarity is always an illusion

explanation.gentle: The chapter says the story can match while the structure differs.
explanation.direct: Narrative compression can preserve the headline resemblance while hiding different risk and capability underneath.
explanation.competitive: The title can match even while the chassis changes completely.

questions.prompt: What deeper shift does the chapter ask from the reader?
choices: Move from rhetorical comparison to structural comparison
Assume that labels are always deceptive
Stop comparing anything with anything else

explanation.gentle: The chapter changes how the reader judges sameness.
explanation.direct: Taleb wants comparison to follow capability, exposure, and payoff rather than stop at narrative likeness.
explanation.competitive: Stop trusting the badge and start auditing the build.

questions.prompt: How does this chapter lead into the next one?
choices: It argues that present labels are more reliable than retrospective stories
It shows that if present comparison already flattens difference, retrospective history can flatten it even more
It proves that history should replace present analysis

explanation.gentle: The next chapter asks how history erases what really happened even more aggressively.
explanation.direct: The bridge is from false equivalence in the present to retrospective narrative that writes from the wrong angle.
explanation.competitive: If the label lies now, tomorrow's history can harden the lie.
